A confidential United Nations report circulated to member states on Wednesday states that Iran increased its stockpile of uranium enriched to near weapons‑grade levels before Israel launched air strikes on 13 June. The report notes that this figure is based on information provided by Iran, agency verification activities between 17 May 2025 and 12 June 2025, and estimates derived from past operation of the relevant facilities. The material is a short, technical step away from weapons‑grade levels of 90%. The report also says Iran and the IAEA have not reached an agreement on resuming inspections of sites affected by Israeli and U.S. bombings in June, with the only site inspected since the conflict being the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant, which operates with Russian technical assistance. In the report, IAEA Director‑General Rafael Grossi said, 'technical modalities to enable the full resumption of Agency inspection should be concluded without delay.' He added that Tehran’s decision to stop cooperation with the IAEA was 'deeply regrettable.' The IAEA has not been able to conduct the in‑field activities required to collect and verify Iran’s declarations used to estimate changes to the previously reported stockpile since 13 June. According to the IAEA, approximately 42 kilograms of 60% enriched uranium is theoretically enough to produce one atomic bomb if further enriched to 90%. The IAEA also reported that inspectors have not verified Iran’s near bomb‑grade stockpile for over two and a half months, a matter it called 'a matter of serious concern.' Iran has long insisted its program is peaceful, though it is the only non‑nuclear‑armed nation enriching uranium to those levels. The U.S., the IAEA and others assess that Iran had a nuclear weapons programme up until 2003.

The agency highlighted that it has not been able to confirm Iran’s near‑bomb‑level stockpile for more than two and a half months, describing this as a 'ciddi bir endişe konusu.' Iran continues to claim its program is peaceful, yet it remains the only country that has enriched uranium to these levels without possessing nuclear weapons.

articles.title: IAEA Demands Iran Allow Verification of Enriched Uranium Stockpile Amid Escalating Tensions
articles.summary: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has urged Iran to allow verification of its stockpile of enriched uranium, particularly highly enriched uranium, according to two unannounced reports. The IAEA stated that information on previously declared nuclear materials in Iran has been cut off since the damage to facilities during the 12-day conflict in June 2024, when Israel and the United States conducted strikes on Iranian nuclear sites. Iran reportedly possessed approximately 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% purity as of June 13, 2024, but has since been unable to verify this stockpile. The IAEA described Iran’s stock of high-enriched uranium as a 'serious concern,' noting that the delay in verification—over five months—has been 'too long.' The agency emphasized the need for immediate access to verify declared nuclear materials to alleviate concerns and ensure compliance with safeguards under the Non-Proliferation Treaty, particularly regarding the potential diversion of materials from peaceful use. Iran claims it has permitted IAEA inspectors to visit nuclear sites, with a visit occurring the previous week, according to Foreign Ministry spokesperson Ismail Baghaei. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh also stated that the U.S. has sent contradictory messages about nuclear talks through third parties.

articles.title: Iran Increased Stockpile of near Weapons-grade Uranium before Israeli Attack, UN Agency Says
articles.summary: A confidential report from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) revealed that, as of June 13, 2025, Iran had amassed 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched to 60%, a 32.3‑kilogram (71.2‑pound) rise since the agency’s last May assessment. The report also notes that Iran’s total stockpile of enriched uranium reached 9,874.9 kilograms, up 627.3 kilograms from the previous month. The IAEA highlighted that about 42 kilograms of 60‑percent enriched uranium could theoretically produce a single atomic bomb if further enriched to 90 percent. The report states that inspectors have been unable to verify Iran’s near‑bomb‑grade stockpile for more than two and a half months, describing the situation as a ‘matter of serious concern.’ It further reports that inspections have been suspended following Israeli and U.S. attacks, with only the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant inspected since the war. The IAEA director general, Rafael Grossi, urged that ‘technical modalities to enable the full resumption of Agency inspection should be concluded without delay,’ and the report described Tehran’s decision to cut cooperation with the IAEA as ‘deeply regrettable.’

articles.title: IAEA Demands Uranium Inspections in Iran
articles.summary: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the United Nations' nuclear energy agency, has demanded that Iran allow inspectors to verify its stockpiles of enriched uranium, specifically targeting sites where highly enriched uranium may be stored. The request was made on Wednesday, based on confidential documents revealing that IAEA has lost continuity in monitoring Iran's nuclear program, particularly at facilities damaged during the June conflict with Israel, when U.S. forces attacked suspected sites. According to a prior IAEA report, Iran possessed approximately 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent as of June 13. Uranium must be enriched to 90 percent to be usable in nuclear weapons. The IAEA expressed significant concern over Iran's past access to such quantities of enriched uranium, underscoring the urgency of the new inspection demands.
